'''Veṇvāroha''' is a work in [[Sanskrit]] composed by [[Madhava of Sangamagrama|Mādhava  of Sangamagrāma]] ({{circa|1350}} – {{circa|1425}}), the founder of the [[Kerala school of astronomy and mathematics]]. It is a work in 74 verses describing methods for the computation of the true positions of the [[Moon]] at intervals of about half an hour for various days in an [[Moon cycle|anomalistic cycle]]. This work is an elaboration of an earlier and shorter work of Mādhava himself titled ''[[Sphuta-chandrapti|Sphutacandrāpti]]''.<ref name="Pingree">{{cite book|author=David Edwin Pingree|title=Census of the exact sciences in Sanskrit|publisher=[[American Philosophical Society]]|location=Philadelphia|date=1981|volume=4|pages=414 |isbn=0-87169-146-9}}</ref> ''Veṇvāroha'' is the most popular astronomical work of Mādhava.<ref>{{cite book|editor=Helaine Selin|editor-link=Helaine Selin|title=Encyclopaedia of the History of Science, Technology, and Medicine in Non-Western Cultures |publisher=Springer|date=1997|pages=522|chapter=Article by R.C. Gupta|isbn=978-0-7923-4066-9}}</ref>

==Etymology==
The title ''Veṇvāroha'' literally means '[[Bamboo]] Climbing' (''Veṇu'' 'bamboo' + ''āroha'' 'climbing') and it is indicative of the computational procedure expounded in the text. The computational scheme is like climbing a bamboo tree, going up and up step by step at measured equal heights.

==Overview== 
It is dated 1403 [[Common Era|CE]]. [[Achyuta Pisharati|Acyuta Piṣārati]] (1550–1621), another prominent [[mathematician]]/[[astronomer]] of the [[Kerala school of astronomy and mathematics|Kerala school]], has composed a [[Malayalam]] [[Close reading|commentary]] on ''Veṇvāroha''.<ref name="Pingree"/> This astronomical treatise is of a type generally described as Karaṇa texts in [[India]]. Such works are characterized by the fact that they are compilations of [[algorithm|computational methods]] of [[astronomy|practical astronomy]].
 
The novelty and ingenuity of the method attracted the attention of several of the followers of Mādhava and they composed similar texts thereby creating a genre of works in Indian mathematical tradition  collectively referred to as ‘veṇvāroha texts’. These include ''Drik-veṇvārohakriya'' of unknown authorship of epoch 1695 and ''Veṇvārohastaka'' of [[Puthumana Somayaji|Putuman Somāyaji]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.new.dli.ernet.in/rawdataupload/upload/insa/INSA_1/20005b5e_1.pdf|author=K.V. Sarma|title=A survey of source materials|publisher=Indian national Academy of Science|access-date=21 March 2010|archive-date=11 January 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110111002139/http://www.new.dli.ernet.in/rawdataupload/upload/insa/INSA_1/20005b5e_1.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In the technical terminology of astronomy, the ingenuity introduced by Mādhava in ''Veṇvāroha'' can be explained thus: Mādhava has endeavored   to compute the true [[longitude]] of the Moon by making use of the true motions rather than the epicyclic astronomy of the [[Aryabhata]] tradition. He made  use of the anomalistic revolutions for computing the true positions of the [[Moon]] using the successive true daily velocity specified in ''[[Candravakyas|Candravākyas]]'' (Table of Moon-mnemonics) for easy memorization and use.<ref>{{cite journal|author=K. Chandra Hari|title=Computation of the true moon by Madhava of Sangamagrama|journal=Indian Journal of History of Science|volume=38|issue=3|pages=251–253|url=http://www.new.dli.ernet.in/rawdataupload/upload/insa/INSA_1/2000c4df_231.pdf|access-date=21 March 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120316083104/http://www.new.dli.ernet.in/rawdataupload/upload/insa/INSA_1/2000c4df_231.pdf|archive-date=16 March 2012|url-status=dead|df=dmy-all}}</ref>

Veṇvāroha has been studied from a modern perspective and the process is explained using the properties of periodic functions.<ref>{{cite journal|author=S. Madhavan|title=Veṇvāroha From a Modern Perspective|journal=Indian Journal of History of Science|volume=47|issue=4|pages=699–717|date=2012|url=http://www.insa.nic.in/writereaddata/UpLoadedFiles/IJHS/Vol47_4_8_SMadhavan.pdf}}</ref>
